source_metadata.title: Topical gel-based biomaterials for the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aimed to identify topical biomaterial gel treatment approaches for chronic diabetic wound healing in animal models and clinical trials.
For this review, topical biomaterial gels were defined as injectable viscous gel materials that can be applied to a wound with syringes, pipettes, tubes, or similar methods.
The review excluded biomaterial wound dressings and highly cross-linked preformed hydrogels that require surgical implantation.
The review reports a global diabetic foot ulcer prevalence of 6.3%, with higher prevalence in type 2 diabetes (6.4%) than type 1 diabetes (5.5%).
The review reports diabetic foot ulcer recurrence rates of 40% within 1 year, 60% within 3 years, and 65% within 5 years after healing.
Normal wound healing is described as overlapping phases of hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and re-epithelialization/tissue remodeling.
Chronic wounds are described as abnormal cellular and molecular interactions that produce persistent, self-perpetuating inflammation, particularly affecting the extracellular matrix.
The review states that macrophages in chronic wounds remain in a pro-inflammatory state and have reduced ability to remove neutrophils, debris, and apoptotic cells.
The review describes persistent TNF-alpha and matrix metalloproteinase activity as contributors to extracellular-matrix disruption and impaired diabetic wound healing.
The review identifies poor tissue perfusion, denervation, hyperglycemia, and other diabetes-related comorbidities as contributors to the multifactorial pathophysiology of chronic diabetic wounds.
Natural biomaterial gels discussed in the review include collagen, gelatin, silk, chitosan, cellulose, alginate, hyaluronic acid, chitin, elastin, and decellularized extracellular matrix.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review describes collagen as a common extracellular-matrix component used in wound biomaterials, with biological compatibility but potential variability and processing limitations.

source_anchor.paragraph: Comparison of Topical Gels Used in Wound Healing Applications

atoms.canonical_statement: The review describes gelatin as a denatured collagen-derived biomaterial that can be crosslinked for wound-healing applications.

source_anchor.paragraph: Comparison of Topical Gels Used in Wound Healing Applications

atoms.canonical_statement: The review describes chitosan as a biomaterial used for wound-healing gels because of properties that include biocompatibility and antimicrobial activity.

source_anchor.paragraph: Comparison of Topical Gels Used in Wound Healing Applications

atoms.canonical_statement: Synthetic biomaterial gels discussed in the review include PEG, polyurethane, PLA, PLGA, PCL, Pluronic F127, and zwitterionic polymers, which allow tunable mechanical and degradation properties.

source_anchor.paragraph: Comparison of Topical Gels Used in Wound Healing Applications

atoms.canonical_statement: The review notes that synthetic gel systems can provide more control over crosslinking, degradation, and release behavior, while material bioactivity and tissue interaction remain design tradeoffs.

population.label: patients with diabetic foot ulcers

atoms.canonical_statement: The review identifies Regranex as the only topical gel then FDA approved specifically for diabetic foot ulcer treatment.

The review states that only a select few topical gel approaches had reached human clinical trials, with limited cellular-therapy survival, unknown long-term nanoparticle effects, and FDA trial cost and duration cited as translational barriers.

source_anchor.paragraph: Topical gels applied in clinical settings

atoms.canonical_statement: The review notes that topical gels can have limited mechanical properties and rapid degradation, motivating development of stimulus-responsive or smart hydrogels.

The review identifies material choice, manufacturing complexity, purification, raw-material supply and cost, storage, stability, packaging, regulatory requirements, and multi-component formulation complexity as barriers to clinical translation.
The work was supported by National Institutes of Health funding listed in the acknowledgments.
